In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the increase in plasma NEFA is the result of a massive release of FFA from adipose tissue, which is caused by a marked increase in plasma catecholamines.
the increase of plasma FFA during an ACS is not a primary event but rather a consequence of the release of catecholamines and the activation of lipolysis in adipose tissue.

the increase in plasma NEFA in the first 2–4 h of an ACS is an important marker for the development of serious ventricular fibrillation and that the plasma NEFA level at this time is an important predictor of mortality in the first few hours after an ACS.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ACS is a disorder of lipid metabolism, in which the plasma FFA are the most important lipids.
we were able to show that the plasma FFA level was elevated during the first 24 h of the acute coronary syndrome, but that it was not elevated in the subsequent 24 h.

the FFA hypothesis was born in a series of studies in patients with myocardial infarction, and in the first study we found that FFA concentrations in plasma were elevated in the early stages of infarction, with a peak at 2-3 h after onset, which was not seen in patients with unstable angina.
The main takeaway from our work is that
plasma FFA levels increase within 1 or two hours of the onset of ACS.
the FFA-ACS association is a robust one, but that the mechanism is still unclear.
the elevation of FFA is a consequence of the ACS and not the cause of the ACS.
